processing: An unoxidised green tea. Little is documented specifically for this name; Kaiyang selenium green tea is machine-finished with heat-fixing and shaping.
harvest_season: Not specifically recorded; spring is the usual prized picking for Kaiyang greens.
appearance_dry: Kaiyang selenium greens are described as even and glossy green, with plenty of white down at Nanlong; nothing is recorded for this name alone.
appearance_liquor: Bright green, as described for Kaiyang selenium tea generally.
taste_profile: Tasting notes for this name are scarce. Kaiyang selenium tea is described as fresh and mellow, with some astringency and a clean finish.

brewing.notes: General guidance for a Guizhou green, not a recorded local method. Shorten the steeps if the astringency builds.

vintage_note: Little is recorded about this label's sales. As is usual for Chinese greens, look for the current spring harvest and drink it within the year.
description:
Nangonghe Lü Cha is a green tea from Kaiyang county, north of Guiyang in Guizhou. The Nangong in its name means southern tribute, and the tea is closely tied to the older name Nangong tea from Nanlong township, although the exact relation between the two labels is not well documented.

Kaiyang's whole identity as a tea county rests on selenium in its soil, and that is how this tea is marketed. Reports on the county say 99.91 percent of its soil is rich in selenium; take the health language around it with some caution.

For the cup, descriptions of Kaiyang selenium tea point to a bright green liquor and a fresh, mellow taste with some grip. Treat that as a guide to the area, not a description of this label. Water at about 85°C with short early steeps is a good start.

When buying, check the harvest date and who made it, since this is a local name with little independent description behind it.
history:
The tribute story comes in more than one version. A local account of this tea cites the Wanli-era Guizhou gazetteer for 400 years of tribute tea in Kaiyang, while other accounts say the Nangong name dates from the Qianlong reign of the Qing, when the tea served as a tribute or the emperor is said to have given the name. Treat these as local tradition.

The modern record is firmer: Kaiyang green tea now has national geographical indication status and was named among nationally renowned new agricultural products in 2023.
